Independently re-traced at pristine HEAD (confidential-sync 4acbf16, tinfoil-webapp c061681, tinfoil-buckets-sidecar b89fcc1); every file:line claim holds.

Enclave: internal/server/attachment_ops.go:94-133 derives BOTH the attachment id (18 bytes, info 'tinfoil-attachment-id-v1') and the 32-byte slot key (info 'tinfoil-attachment-key-v1') with HKDF-SHA256, salt=nil, over encodeIKM(idempotencyKey, chatID, clerkSubject, hex(sha256(plaintext))). No CEK, enclave secret or random value is mixed in (the design comment at :45 even says 'No CEK material flows on this request'). AttachmentPut (:208) calls it with the caller's idempotency key; :218/:224 then send (attachment id, chat id, clerk sub) to the controlplane via ReservePendingAttachmentWrite/RegisterAttachmentIndex (controlplane/client.go:1347-1357, 1455-1465, postAttachmentChatID :1472-1500). AttachmentGet (:267-309) is session-agnostic: it resolves the owner from the CP (client.go:1766-1800, service-secret auth only) and calls Buckets.Get(owner, id, attKey). http.go:123-124 registers POST /v1/attachment/get-public with only a timeout wrapper (no authMiddleware), and tinfoil-config.yml shim.paths exposes it (enforced by TestShimPathsMatchRoutes).

Fork path: fork_ops.go:277-281 re-uploads every source attachment with IdempotencyKey = forkAttachmentIdemKey(req.IdempotencyKey, sourceAttachmentID, index) = hex(sha256('fork-att:'+forkIdem+':'+srcAttID+':'+idx))[:16] (:300-303). The same raw req.IdempotencyKey is passed to Push (:124-132), which forwards it verbatim as X-Idempotency-Key on PUT /api/sync/blob/chat/{targetId} (ops.go Push -> PutBlobRequest.IdempotencyKey; controlplane/client.go:426-428). internal/crypto/ophash.go:17 states the CP stores that value in sync_idempotency_keys. The source attachment id is the enclave-minted id (webapp cloud-storage.ts:553 sets att.id = enclaveID; the enclave parses it from json:"id" in import_native.go:95-105 and uses it as the buckets object key at fork_ops.go:262), which the CP already holds in its attachment index and also receives on every chat push via X-Attachment-Refs. Hence for a forked attachment the key is F(CP-visible metadata, plaintext).

Webapp reachability: chat-interface.tsx:2809-2810 (signed in) -> chat-storage.ts:678 cloudSync.forkChat (when cloud sync enabled and the chat is not local-only) -> cloud-sync.ts:806-810 sends idempotencyKey: newIdempotencyKey() (sync-api.ts:1372-1379, random 128-bit, no secret) in the /v1/sync/fork body (sync-api.ts:943-959). Import paths (import_ops.go:294/434-437, import_native.go:690-693) use idem = sha256('import-att:'+chatID+':'+archiveRef+':'+idx)[:16]; chat ids come from importer opts.id(stableKey, createdAt) and are CP-visible as blob paths, but the archive ref is not CP-visible, so imports are a weaker secondary path.

Sidecar: MultiTenantResolver.java:58 turns X-Tinfoil-Encryption-Key into a raw SecretKeySpec and S3Clients.java:25-27 seals with S3EncryptionClient.builderV4().aesKey(key); the object is protected by exactly the derived key (an AWS-account holder could even skip get-public and decrypt S3 objects directly).

Neutraliser search: no salt/secret input, no rate limit on get-public, no CP-side check the enclave relies on for get-public besides owner resolution, no feature flag (DOCUMENT_ATTACHMENT_WRITES_ENABLED is true; image v2 uploads are unconditional), and HEAD 4acbf16 (2026-10-05, the only commit touching this derivation; repos fast-forwarded 2026-10-08) is the latest code, so no fixed release exists. The hunter's work copy differs from pristine only by a CP request-observer hook in internal/localstack/stack.go plus the two PoC test files.

Reproduction: I copied the pristine repo into my verify directory, added only the observer hook and the PoC test, and ran `go test -tags=smoke -run TestPoC_ -v -count=1 ./internal/localstack/smoke` (Go 1.27.1): PASS, same ids/keys as the hunter's run (unauthenticated get-public returned the plaintext for both the first upload and the CP-derived fork copy; wrong key -> 400). I also wrote my own Python HKDF re-derivation (scripts/rederive.py, run with python3 -I) that reproduces the enclave-minted id 81c9505e... and key HsyBkY5q... and the fork copy's CP-visible id ad2028d2... from public inputs only.

Impact assessment: Tinfoil's controlplane operator (or anyone with CP DB/log read access) can, for every forked attachment, confirm offline whether the plaintext equals a candidate file (derived id == chat_attachments.id, no enclave call, scalable across users) and recover the bytes of any guessable/low-entropy attachment through the credential-free get-public route or directly from S3. This contradicts the README promise that 'neither Tinfoil nor the storage layer can read chats'. High-entropy, unknown files stay protected and the attack needs a privileged CP position plus a user-initiated fork, so Medium (not High) is correct; the PoC is solid and the confirmation-of-file impact is unambiguous, which meets the brief's bar for a reportable Medium. Not a duplicate of the five known findings (all transport/attestation/snapshot issues).

(3) A unit test in a pristine copy calling the shipped deriveAttachmentMaterials/forkAttachmentIdemKey yields the same id/key; offline confirmation runs at ~400k candidates/s per core (Go), ~156k/s in Python. SEVERITY (the point of this review): Attacker = Tinfoil's control-plane operator (api.tinfoil.sh, closed source) or anyone with read access to the CP database (sync_idempotency_keys, chat_attachments) or CP request logs; no user credential, CEK, enclave, TLS or storage-layer compromise is needed; the optional byte retrieval is unauthenticated from any internet client. No other party can mount it (S3 holder lacks chat id/idempotency key; TLS terminates inside the CVM). Single deployment mode: Tinfoil Chat cloud sync enabled; affected objects are attachment copies minted by the enclave when a synced chat is branched (chat-interface.tsx:2810 -> chat-storage.ts:678 -> cloudSync.forkChat -> enclave /v1/sync/fork, always when isCloudSyncEnabled()) or imported (practically native-backup restores: archive path attachments/<CP-visible id>/<filename>; ChatGPT/Claude exports carry random vendor file ids so they are not realistically derivable). Outcome: silent, offline confirmation that a victim's forked/imported attachment equals an attacker-supplied candidate (a cross-user scan for a specific document costs one SHA-256 + HKDF per candidate and never touches the enclave), and recovery of enumerable content: document payloads are JSON {"textContent":"<verbatim file text>"} / pages (document-payload.ts, DOCUMENT_ATTACHMENT_WRITES_ENABLED: true at HEAD), so known public/leaked text documents and very short text files are confirmable/brute-forceable. Net: real, reproduced, PoC solid, impact a partial but unambiguous confidentiality break against the product's primary adversary for a defined class of data -> Medium (low end). I could not push it to Low: the capability is cheap, silent, scalable across all users, and exactly the class the designers themselves guard against elsewhere. I could not push it to High: it leaks nothing about unguessable content and needs CP-side data.

candidate.title: tinfoil-rs: an EHBP proxy can silently truncate streamed completions (prefix of authenticated frames accepted as a complete response)
candidate.component: tinfoil-rs HEAD 084df40 (crate `tinfoil` 0.2.1): src/sse.rs:43-110 (`parse_event_stream` ends on transport EOF; L133 drops `[DONE]` without requiring it), src/relaxed.rs:69-89 (`create_stream`), src/ehbp_transport.rs:269-302 (`EhbpProxy::send`) and src/client.rs:746-753 (EhbpTransport wired into async-openai 0.41.1, whose `stream()` in registry src/client.rs ends at EOF). Pinned EHBP client tinfoil-ehbp 0.3.1 (git rev 93cc1fa): rust/src/client.rs:951-968 `decrypt_response_stream` + rust/src/derive.rs:201-208 `ResponseDecryptor::finish` only reject EOF inside a frame. EHBP SPEC.md 6.2.1 explicitly delegates application-level completion to the application, which the SDK does not implement.
candidate.attacker_position: Proxy mode only (`Client::new_with_proxy` / `SecureClient::new_with_proxy`, the mode whose whole purpose is an untrusted intermediary): the operator of the EHBP proxy, or whoever terminates the client<->proxy TLS connection (for `http://127.0.0.1:` proxies, any process that can bind/intercept that loopback port). The attacker needs no key material: EHBP frames are `LEN||ciphertext` in the clear, so it forwards any prefix of the enclave's authenticated frames and ends the HTTP body cleanly (Content-Length or terminating chunk). Direct TLS-pinned mode is NOT affected (the TLS peer is the enclave; a network attacker's TCP cut surfaces as a TLS/HTTP framing error).
candidate.preconditions: Application uses proxy mode and a streaming API: `chat().create_stream()` (async-openai typed path), `chat_relaxed().create_stream()`, or `sse::parse_event_stream`. Non-streaming JSON responses are not affected (truncated JSON fails to parse; shown as control).
candidate.root_cause: The EHBP layer authenticates each frame but has no end-of-message marker (SPEC 4.3: 'End of message is indicated by the end of the HTTP entity body'); tinfoil-ehbp rust/src/derive.rs:201-208 `finish()` only checks that EOF falls on a frame boundary. The SDK's streaming consumers then treat EOF as the end of the completion: src/sse.rs:125-140 `parse_event_block` skips `data: [DONE]` instead of requiring it, and src/sse.rs:97-109 drains the buffer and ends the stream without error when the byte stream ends; the typed path uses async-openai's eventsource stream which likewise ends at EOF (`execute_stream` -> `stream()`), and src/ehbp_transport.rs:269-302 returns the decrypted stream straight through. No path checks for `[DONE]` or a `finish_reason` before completing.
candidate.impact: Integrity of model output for proxy-mode users: the proxy can cut a streamed answer at any SSE event boundary, including dropping a trailing safety qualification ('NO. Do not proceed.'), dropping a tool_call delta so an agent never executes the requested tool, dropping `finish_reason`, or returning an empty completion (0 frames). The client sees a normal stream end with no error, so neither the application nor the user can tell the answer was cut. Confidentiality is unaffected (the proxy never learns plaintext). Contradicts EHBP SPEC 7.1 'Response forgery'/7.2 expectations as applied by the SDK; the spec itself (6.2.1) says completion MUST be established by the application, which the SDK is.

candidate.root_cause: go-tdx-guest's getTcbInfo/getQeIdentity (verify/verify.go:371-440) parse one HTTP body twice with different semantics. (1) `json.Unmarshal(body, &collateral.TdxTcbInfo)` (encoding/json v1) matches object members case-insensitively and decodes later members into the same struct field in place, so `{"tcbInfo": <genuine>, "tcbinfo": <forged>, "signature": <genuine>}` yields TcbInfo = genuine with every member present in the forged object overridden (tcbLevels/tdxModuleIdentities/nextUpdate/fmspc/tdxModule...; for QE Identity: mrsigner/isvprodid/attributes/miscselect/tcbLevels/nextUpdate). (2) `bodyToRawMessage("tcbInfo", body)` builds `map[string]json.RawMessage` and returns the exact-key member, so collateral.TcbInfoBody is the genuine signed bytes and verifyResponse's `signingCertificate.CheckSignature(ECDSAWithSHA256, rawBody, sig)` succeeds. Everything enforced afterwards (checkTcbInfoTcbStatus, verifyTdQuoteBody, verifyQeReport, checkCollateralExpiration) reads the merged struct. tinfoil-go wraps the library without re-checking: pcsReplayGetter hands the body through unchanged (authenticate.go:170-201) and the tcbEvaluationRecorder decodes with encoding/json/v2, which is case-sensitive and ignores unknown members, so it records the genuine evaluation number (policy floor 19 is satisfied by the genuine value 20) and nothing rejects the extra member. Exact duplicate keys are NOT exploitable in Go (v1 applies last-wins to both the struct and the raw map, so the forged copy fails the signature; control test included) — the Go mechanism is case folding, which is why the known tinfoil-python finding's statement that 'Go/V3 is not affected' is wrong.

candidate.attacker_position: Two capabilities are needed. (A) Serve or alter the attestation bundle the JS client consumes: the operator of atc.tinfoil.sh (default SecureClient/TinfoilAI flow, Tinfoil-operated and unattested), the operator of github-proxy.tinfoil.sh (Verifier.verify()/assembleAttestationBundle flow), a WebPKI-capable on-path MitM of those hosts, or whoever controls a custom attestationBundleURL. (B) A DSSE signature made with ANY Fulcio-issued certificate ever bearing repository=tinfoilsh/confidential-model-router and ref=refs/tags/* -- i.e. the ephemeral signing key of any past tagged release-workflow run (compromised runner, third-party action or dependency at any point in the past; GitHub; or a Fulcio/Sigstore CA compromise). Fulcio chain, SCT and DSSE signature are still enforced, so the cert itself must be genuine. With a correct verifier such a key is usable only inside its 10-minute validity window and only with a public Rekor record; with tinfoil-js (sigstore-browser <= 0.1.14) it is usable indefinitely and silently. To convert forged provenance into prompt decryption the attacker additionally runs their own AMD SEV-SNP Genoa VM (genuine VCEK-signed report, debug off, TSME on) with the forged snp_measurement and their own HPKE key; the SDK then encrypts requests to that key. Same for all deployment modes (ehbp default, tls, browser) since the sigstore step is shared.

Attacker possesses a Fulcio leaf cert + private key with the repo/tag-ref claims (SCT and Fulcio chain still verified). Attacker can deliver the bundle (ATC / github-proxy / MitM / custom attestationBundleURL). For full confidentiality impact: attacker-controlled SEV-SNP Genoa machine satisfying the JS policy (reportedTcb >= bl 7/snp 0xe/ucode 0x48, debug=0, migrate=0, TSME enabled) -- not tested on hardware.
candidate.root_cause: @freedomofpress/sigstore-browser 0.1.14 src/sigstore.ts verifyDsse (:823-947) delegates tlog checks to verifyInclusionPromise (:399-588) and verifyInclusionProof (:590-612). verifyInclusionPromise only verifies a SET if `entry.inclusionPromise?.signedEntryTimestamp` is present (:449) and otherwise merely requires that *some* inclusionProof object exists; it then trusts the unsigned `entry.integratedTime` to check certificate validity (:503-511, repeated at :909-921). verifyInclusionProof recomputes the Merkle root from the attacker-supplied hashes/treeSize/logIndex (verifyMerkleInclusion, trivially satisfiable with treeSize=1, logIndex=0, hashes=[], rootHash=leafHash) and verifies the checkpoint signature only `if (entry.inclusionProof.checkpoint)` (:607). No code path requires a Rekor signature, the logId is never matched against the trusted root in that path, and tsaThreshold is 0. tinfoil-js packages/verifier/src/sigstore.ts:97 calls verifyDsse and adds no tlog check of its own, so a bundle whose only genuine material is the Fulcio leaf + DSSE signature passes verifyCode and Verifier.verifyBundle sets securityVerified=true (client.ts:58-115). Upstream 0.1.15 (e8d5d67) added assertBundle (checkpoint envelope required) and per-entry SET/checkpoint verification, which rejects the PoC; tinfoil-js still declares ^0.1.14 and locks 0.1.14.
candidate.impact: The transparency-log stage of code-provenance verification is void for affected installs: any bundle with a genuine Fulcio leaf and a DSSE signature by its key is accepted with securityVerified=true even though no Rekor key signed anything and the 'signing time' is attacker-chosen inside the cert window. Consequences: (1) an ephemeral Fulcio signing key from any past tagged release run of tinfoilsh/confidential-model-router (10-minute cert) becomes a permanent, unlogged signing capability for arbitrary in-toto statements, i.e. arbitrary snp_measurement values; combined with an attacker-run SEV-SNP enclave this makes the SDK accept non-measured code and encrypt user prompts (EHBP) to the attacker's HPKE key, or pin TLS to the attacker's key in tls mode; (2) Sigstore's detectability property (every accepted signature is publicly logged) is lost for JS clients, so a release-pipeline compromise can be exploited later without leaving a Rekor record. Demonstrated end to end at the public API: SecureClient.ready() against a loopback ATC serving the forged bundle resolves with securityVerified=true and all steps 'success'. Not a standalone break: without a Fulcio-issued key the Fulcio chain + SCT checks still hold.

Code trace (pristine tinfoil-js HEAD bedbe69): packages/verifier/src/sigstore.ts:68-97 builds `new SigstoreVerifier()` with default options, loads the bundled trusted root, rejects only the legacy x509CertificateChain layout (:79-83) and then relies entirely on `verifier.verifyDsse(bundle, policy)` (:97); no tlog check of Tinfoil's own exists anywhere in packages/*/src (grep for rekor/tlog/inclusion/checkpoint hits only comments). client.ts:70-78 sets verifyCode=success and :124 securityVerified=true on return. packages/tinfoil/src/atc.ts and secure-client.ts:269-295 pass the ATC JSON (sigstoreBundle, digest, releaseTag) straight into verifyBundle with no cross-check. The published @tinfoilsh/verifier@1.2.2 dist is byte-identical to my fresh build of HEAD (diff -r); tinfoil@1.2.2 dist differs only in ai-sdk-provider.js. sigstore-browser 0.1.14 (tarball from npm, sha256 69a37776...): src/sigstore.ts verifyInclusionPromise :399-588 verifies a SET only inside `if (!entry.inclusionPromise?.signedEntryTimestamp) {...} else {...}` (:449); otherwise it only requires that some inclusionProof object exists, then anchors cert validity on the unsigned entry.integratedTime (:507). verifyInclusionProof :590-612 recomputes the Merkle root from attacker-supplied hashes/treeSize/logIndex (:605, tlog/merkle.ts: treeSize=1, logIndex=0, hashes=[], rootHash=SHA256(0x00||body) passes) and calls verifyCheckpoint only `if (entry.inclusionProof.checkpoint)` (:607). verifyDsse :823-947 repeats the unsigned integratedTime check (:911); tsaThreshold defaults to 0 (:103); tlogThreshold=1 is satisfied by entry count alone; logId is never compared with the trusted root on this path. dist/sigstore.js (:312,:355,:440,:652) matches src. SDK level with my own loopback HTTPS ATC and self-signed cert: `new SecureClient({attestationBundleURL})` -> ready() resolves, securityVerified=true, all five steps success, request logged as tinfoil-js/1.2.2. Swapping node_modules to 0.1.15 (npm tarball): every attack variant rejected ("Invalid bundle: inclusion proof" from the new assertBundle, which requires inclusionProof.checkpoint.envelope, plus per-entry verifySET/verifyCheckpoint in verifyTlogEntries :344-389 with observer-timestamp enforcement); 0.1.11 accepts like 0.1.14. candidate.root_cause: On KeyConfigMismatchError the re-verifying transport re-attests (genuinely) and then calls `retry_inner.handle_request(request)` with the SAME httpx.Request whose stream was already consumed by the first, encrypted attempt (client.py wheel L445 / L488). tinfoil-ehbp's transport decides 'bodyless' purely by peeking the stream (transport.py L170-178: `encrypted = self._identity.encrypt_request_stream(request.stream)`; `if encrypted is None: ... _bodyless_passthrough(request)`), deliberately ignoring Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding. CODE CLAIMS: confirmed with my own evidence, not the hunter's. I built a fresh venv from PyPI (tinfoil==0.14.0 resolves tinfoil-ehbp 0.4.0; httpx 0.28.1; openai 3.26.0), verified the wheel sha256s against PyPI metadata, and diffed the wheels against repo HEAD: `_EHBPReVerifyingTransport`/`_AsyncEHBPReVerifyingTransport` are byte-identical (client.py differs only in version lookup) and ehbp transport.py/identity.py/_http.py are identical to encrypted-http-body-protocol 7ee9288. Unlike the hunter's PoC (which instantiated `_EHBPReVerifyingTransport` directly, even in the case labelled "make_secure_http_client()"), my PoC drives the real public API: `SecureClient(..., transport="ehbp", base_url=<loopback>).make_secure_http_client()` / `make_secure_async_http_client()` with only `verify()` stubbed, so the full shipped stack runs (cache-secret injector, X-Tinfoil-Enclave-Url, host binding, re-verifying transport, EHBPTransport, httpx.HTTPTransport). Result (verify_poc.log): 14/14 one-shot shapes (open(file,'rb'), io.BytesIO, iter([...]), async iterable object; both /v1/chat/completions and /v1/embeddings; with and without a user_cache_secret) sent request 2 with no Ehbp-Encapsulated-Key, Content-Length: 0, body_len 0, and the peer's forged nonce-less 200 was returned to the caller as a 200 (verify() was genuinely re-run twice). Controls behave as the hunter says: bytes bodies re-encrypt and raise MissingResponseNonceError; generators raise StreamConsumed. The cache-secret transport does not rescue the case: `_request_with_user_cache_secret` catches `httpx.RequestNotRead` and forwards stream bodies untouched. Root cause verified: client.py L441/L484 retry the SAME httpx.Request; httpx IteratorByteStream re-iterates a file/iterator silently as empty; ehbp transport.py L170-178/L248-253 treat an empty stream as bodyless and return the plaintext response with no nonce check. tinfoil-go refuses this case (recovery_transport.go:63-65), so Python is the odd one out.

REACH (the severity-limiting fact): verify_sdk_paths.log shows every documented high-level surface is NOT affected: openai.OpenAI(http_client=make_secure_http_client()) chat/embeddings (JSON -> ByteStream), audio.transcriptions with a seekable file (httpx re-seeks) and even with a reader lacking seek() (multipart re-renders a non-empty body, retry still encrypted), `NewSecureClient().post(json=/data=)` (dict only, `_HTTPSecureClient.post` has no content= parameter), `SecureClient.post(bytes)`/`make_request`. Across all 100 public repos the only external Python consumer (demo-personalization) uses AsyncTinfoilAI. The vulnerable surface is therefore only a third-party app that calls the raw httpx client from `make_secure_http_client()`/`make_secure_async_http_client()` with a file-like/iterator body (a normal httpx upload idiom, and the docstring explicitly promises the key-rotation retry is safe), which the hunter concedes.

ATTACKER: must be the client's TLS peer, because the forged 422 problem+json and the forged 200 must arrive on the TLS connection; no HPKE key is needed (raise_for_key_config_mismatch runs on any nonce-less 422). In EHBP mode the inner transport is a plain `httpx.HTTPTransport()` (WebPKI, no pin; `_build_ehbp_sync_transport` L728-730), so: base_url/proxy mode = the proxy or gateway operator by design; default direct mode (TinfoilAI/NewSecureClient default to the router enclave) = a publicly trusted certificate for the enclave hostname plus an on-path position (Tinfoil as DNS/host owner, ACME-capable host, CA mis-issuance) - inside Tinfoil's "not even Tinfoil" model, the same position accepted for Findings 1 and 4.

OUTCOME: integrity only. The application receives an attacker-chosen body as the enclave's authenticated reply to a sealed POST, silently, and the user's real request body is never delivered (an honest enclave would just return a pass-through 4xx: functional bug). No confidentiality loss: the exhausted stream sends nothing in plaintext, and headers are plaintext by design. This contradicts SPEC 5.3/5.4.1 ("exchanges that claim success always fail closed without a valid nonce"), SPEC 7.1 (response forgery), and the SDK docstring; the conformance SECURITY-AUDIT "status/headers outside AEAD" limitation does not cover a sealed-to-unsealed downgrade of a request that had a body.

DUPLICATE CHECK: not a duplicate. Finding 4 is Go-only (REPORT.md explicitly lists tinfoil-python as not affected), with a different trigger (303 redirect vs. 422 key-config), different code and a different fix; Finding 1 leaks plaintext and nothing plaintext leaves here. It is the same impact class as Finding 4, so Finding 4's Medium is the ceiling, and the extra body-shape precondition with no shipped consumer puts it at the low end of Medium. Per the grading rule, a real Medium stays unrefuted; a triager who weighs "no shipped Tinfoil code path" as decisive would call it Low, which is the main source of my uncertainty.

The hunter's claims that the JS, Rust and Swift clients are not affected were not re-verified by me (only the Go refusal in recovery_transport.go was checked); they do not affect this verdict. 5. The hunter's "make_secure_http_client().post(content=BytesIO)" case did not actually go through make_secure_http_client(); my PoC closes that gap and confirms the real API is affected, including with the default user_cache_secret injector in place (it forwards unread stream bodies untouched). 6. SDK composition used by the PoC is identical to tinfoil-go enclave_transport.go buildEHBPTransport L137-148 (ehbpclient.NewTransportWithIdentity) under openai-go v3.42.0.
candidate.attacker_position: The client's TLS peer: Tinfoil's unattested gateway or a configured proxy for tinfoil-proxy, confidential-openai-adapter, confidential-tinfoil-harness and any NewGateway/WithBaseURL user (on-path by design); a WebPKI-certificate-capable on-path party in direct-to-enclave EHBP mode. The attacker needs no key material: frame lengths are plaintext (SPEC 7.2), so it cuts exactly on a boundary.
candidate.preconditions: A streamed (multi-frame) response, e.g. SSE chat completions where each flushed SSE event becomes one EHBP frame (httputil.ReverseProxy FlushInterval=-1 in the production shim cvmimage/tinfoil/cmd/shim/api.go, and the Go middleware's Write-per-chunk at identity/crypt.go L282-306). candidate.root_cause: The protocol has no authenticated end-of-message marker and no total-length commitment; every receiver accepts a clean EOF after any number of authenticated frames as a complete message. openai-go's SSE reader ends the stream without error when the body ends without `data: [DONE]`, so the application sees a shorter answer with stream.Err()==nil and no finish_reason.
candidate.impact: Integrity (deletion only): an on-path party can truncate the model's answer at any token/event boundary without detection, e.g. removing a trailing caveat, a tool call, or the end of a code block; the Tinfoil Chat harness acts on streamed tool calls, so dropping the tail changes behaviour. Cannot insert or modify content.

votes.reasoning:
Every technical fact in the candidate re-derives correctly from my own evidence, but the finding is a missing-hardening gap (no Windows Authenticode / publisherName, no .deb signing) whose exploitation requires an attacker who already controls a trust anchor, so it does not meet the brief's "serious vulnerability" bar (which excludes best-practice notes, missing hardening and findings that presuppose a compromised trusted party).

What I confirmed independently (pristine repo HEAD 74d105c; npm tarballs whose sha512 equals the lockfile integrity; release assets I downloaded myself whose sha512/sha256 equal the published latest*.yml/SHA256SUMS):
- app/src/main/updater.ts:13-14 sets autoDownload/autoInstallOnAppQuit, checks on launch and every 6h; index.ts:59 calls it; no cert pinning or TLS weakening anywhere in app/src.
- electron-builder.yml has no win.publisherName/forceCodeSigning; release.yml:111-128 gives Apple signing secrets only to the macOS job, the Windows/Linux job gets GH_TOKEN only.
- electron-updater 6.8.9 NsisUpdater.js:84-100 returns null (skip) when app-update.yml lacks publisherName; BaseUpdater.js:69-89 installs silently (/S) on normal quit; DebUpdater.js:51-57 + LinuxUpdater.js:34-50 run `dpkg -i` via pkexec/sudo; main.js:50-70 picks DebUpdater only when resources/package-type == deb. builder-util-runtime DigestTransform is the only integrity check (sha512 from the same feed). app-builder-lib PublishManager.js:202-208 + windowsSignToolManager.js:18-29 write publisherName only when a signing cert exists.
- Shipped v0.2.3 (current /releases/latest; v0.3.0-rc.2 is prerelease and excluded): Tinfoil-Proxy-Setup.exe, tinfoil-proxy-windows-amd64.exe, the bundled resources/bin/tinfoil-proxy.exe and elevate.exe all have an empty IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_SECURITY (hunter's script and my pefile check agree). resources/app-update.yml inside both the installer and the .deb is owner/repo/provider/releaseType/updaterCacheDirName only. The .deb contains resources/package-type = "deb" and has no signature member.

Why it is not serious under the brief: the only parties who can exploit it are (1) someone with write access to the project's GitHub releases (compromised maintainer/token/CI), i.e. an already-compromised distribution channel — the analogue of the brief's excluded "already-compromised enclave"; (2) a TLS-terminating intermediary whose CA is already in the victim's OS trust store (enterprise MDM/AV), which already administers the device and can replace any download or inject into any site; (3) public-CA mis-issuance for github.com, not a realistic position. A plain on-path attacker cannot exploit it (Chromium net validates against the OS store), as the hunter concedes. The code works as designed (TLS + sha512); the "fix" is adding signing infrastructure. Severity is High only if one assumes the trust anchor is already lost, so no realistic deployment mode reaches the required High/Critical, and the Medium rating rests on a static, non-executed PoC. It remains a sound hardening recommendation to pass to the vendor (sign Windows builds and set win.publisherName so NsisUpdater enforces it; sign the .deb or disable Linux auto-install), but not a reportable vulnerability for this review.

(e) Runtime harness (poc/harness.cjs): the real pinned electron-updater 6.8.9 with the real shipped app-update.yml, pointed at a loopback fake GitHub, accepted a forged feed+latest.yml+payload on both the NSIS and the Deb path, never invoked the Authenticode verifier (0 calls), and on simulated quit produced `<payload>.exe --updated /S` (Windows), `elevate.exe <payload> --updated /S` when the attacker sets isAdminRightsRequired: true in latest.yml (UAC -> admin), and `pkexec ... dpkg -i <payload>.deb` (Linux root). macOS is not affected (MacUpdater hands the zip to Squirrel.Mac, which requires a matching Developer ID signature; the mac build is signed/notarized).

THREAT MODEL / SEVERITY: Exploitation requires one of: (1) write access to release assets of github.com/tinfoilsh/tinfoil-proxy (stolen maintainer/bot token with contents:write can clobber the existing v0.2.3 assets, no tag/branch protection applies; GitHub-side compromise; malicious insider; a malicious dependency in the release job also works but that sub-case also exposes the macOS p12, so CI-held signing would not stop it); (2) a TLS interception position with a root the victim OS trusts (enterprise inspection or a compromised inspection appliance; Electron's net module uses Chromium's stack with the system proxy and OS trust store); (3) CA mis-issuance for github.com. A plain on-path attacker cannot exploit it, and no Tinfoil gateway/enclave component is involved. Within the precondition the outcome is unambiguous: arbitrary code as the user on every Windows desktop-app install (silent install at next quit, preceded only by a benign-looking "update ready" dialog that cannot distinguish a malicious update), root on Linux after a generic polkit password prompt, optional admin on Windows via UAC, for all users within ~6 h; this reads the API key, prompts and responses on the host and so defeats EHBP/attestation for that user. Tinfoil's stated model (enclave attestation, "not even Tinfoil") says nothing about desktop-binary supply chain; the README only says builds auto-update. Not a duplicate: none of findings 1-5 concern the desktop app, electron-updater or release signing. Formal CVSS 3.1 comes out High, but the realistic severity is Medium: the precondition is an already-compromised vendor release channel or an OS-trusted MITM (endpoint-admin-equivalent), the behaviour is electron-updater's documented default for unsigned apps, the desktop app is optional (README steers most users to the CLI/Docker, which the same channel compromise would also hit via install.sh/SHA256SUMS), and a vendor may triage the root cause (no Windows code signing, no Linux package signing) as hardening. It is nevertheless a real CWE-494 weakness with a solid library-level PoC and an unambiguous impact, so it stays reportable at Medium with the attacker position stated exactly. Suggested framing: "supply-chain hardening: desktop auto-update executes unsigned code; integrity rests on GitHub TLS", fix = Authenticode (HSM/cloud key outside CI) + publisherName, disable Linux auto-install or ship a signed apt repo, consider an update-signing key independent of GitHub.

Corrections to the hunter's text: the Linux prompt is the generic polkit prompt for running /bin/bash as root, not a dialog titled "Tinfoil Proxy would like to update" (that string is only passed to kdesudo/gksudo); Linux auto-update is active despite README:189 saying only macOS/Windows auto-update; the CI-dependency sub-case also exposes the macOS signing p12 (CSC_LINK), so CI-held Windows signing would not stop it; the attacker can force elevate.exe/UAC via isAdminRightsRequired. Expect vendor pushback that this is a hardening gap (electron-updater's documented default for unsigned apps); report it as Medium with the exact precondition and the fix (HSM/cloud-key Authenticode + publisherName, disable Linux auto-install or sign an apt repo, optionally an independent update-signing key and autoInstallOnAppQuit=false until then). A possible separate local-privilege variant (user-level process swapping the .deb in the user-writable update cache before the root dpkg -i) was noticed but not assessed or reproduced.

candidate.attacker_position: Any third party who can get text in front of the model: the author of a web page the user asks about (pasted link), a page/snippet that web_search returns (snippets from top-500k hosts are never screened), or a document the user uploads. No account, no network position, no Tinfoil infrastructure needed. Applies to Tinfoil Chat (webapp/iOS via the harness) for signed-in and anonymous users; the legacy /agui API path (API-key callers) is identical. The data leaves the enclave in a URL fetched by Exa's crawler (web_fetch), context.dev (render_link_preview) or the victim's own browser (image URLs), all of which the attacker observes on their web server.
candidate.preconditions: Victim has web search enabled (default: context.go:195, records.go:109, webapp resolveWebSearchEnabled(true,...)) or GenUI widgets enabled (default) for the link-preview/image channels; the model follows the injected instruction (scripted in the PoC, not exercised against production models). Injection page hosted on any registrable domain in Cloudflare Radar top 500k (github.com, gist/raw.githubusercontent.com, medium.com, reddit.com, substack.com, wordpress.com ...) bypasses the websearch classifier entirely; on other hosts the LLM classifier (narrow policy, fail-open) must be evaded.
candidate.root_cause: agent.go:115-127 appends every model tool call to the conversation and runs execute() -> invoke() -> toolset.call() (agent.go:195-274) with no allow-list, confirmation, or URL inspection; the only mitigation is one sentence in the webSearch system prompt (tools.go:55). The websearch fetch handler (handlers.go:202-204) forwards every URL verbatim to Exa /contents with maxAgeHours:2 (fetch.go:130-132), which forces a live crawl of unseen URLs, so an attacker-chosen URL with the conversation in its query string reaches the attacker's server; the PII filter is explicitly disabled for fetch (PIICheckEnabled:false) and the injection classifier is skipped when the host's eTLD+1 is in the top-500k list and the caller sent no X-Tinfoil-Tool-Injection-Check header (service.go:236-251; the harness never sets it, confirmed in websearch.final.log), and is fail-open (service.go:360-364). render_link_preview is executed by the harness itself (widgets.go:66-74) and the metadata enclave scrapes the model-chosen URL through context.dev with maxAgeMs=0 (client.go:68-72), a second channel with no classifier at all. The model context contains the system prompt (personalization, project instructions, project documents, memory) plus the whole history window (context.go:128-231), so all of it is exfiltrable; up to 16 tool turns x 20 URLs per call give ample bandwidth.
candidate.impact: Confidentiality of exactly what Tinfoil Chat promises to protect: the conversation (prior user messages), project documents and system instructions, personalization (nickname, profession, additional context) and any uploaded document text are delivered to an attacker's web server, inside the enclave's normal tool traffic, with a normal-looking answer to the victim. PoC recovered the SSN-bearing prior message, the project document and the personalization block verbatim on the attacker side.

candidate.unverified_assumptions: (1) Production models (kimi-k3, deepseek-v4-flash, gemma4-31b, gpt-oss-120b, llama3-3-70b) follow the injected instruction: the PoC scripts the model; compliance rate not measured (no production traffic allowed). (2) Exa live-crawls an uncached URL when maxAgeHours:2 is sent (documented semantics, emulated locally). (3) github.com/medium.com/etc. are in Cloudflare Radar's top-500k dataset (a 7-domain stub was served locally). (4) The control plane's genUI.enabledWidgets includes render_link_preview/render_image in production (the webapp registers both; harness only offers what the control plane enables).
candidate.suggested_fix: Harness: treat tool-chosen URLs as data egress. Allow web_fetch/render_link_preview/render_image only for URLs that appeared verbatim in the user's messages or in prior web_search results of the same run, drop query strings/fragments and cap URL length otherwise, and require an explicit user resolution (the AG-UI 'resolve' turn already exists) for anything else. Websearch: do not skip the injection classifier for user-content hosts (make the popularity skip opt-in per caller, never default), fail closed when the classifier errors, and run the privacy filter plus a cheap entropy/length check over fetch URLs before sending them to Exa. Metadata enclave: only accept URLs the user supplied. Webapp: do not load model-chosen remote images (proxy or block; drop https: from img-src).
candidate.why_not_known_finding: The five known findings are transport/attestation defects (EHBP plaintext replay, TDX collateral JSON differential, /snapshot auth bypass, 3xx response forgery, summarizer pin ordering) exploited by a TLS peer or host. This is an application-layer data-flow defect in the harness tool loop and the websearch/metadata services, exploitable by any web-page author with no network position; it does not depend on any of the known issues.

votes.reasoning: I re-traced every file:line claim in the pristine repos at HEAD and found no check that neutralises the chain. Harness 4c170c6: agent.go:109-127 appends each model tool call and runs execute()->invoke()->toolset.call() (195-274) with no URL policy, allow-list, or user confirmation (the AG-UI 'resolve' kind in thread.go only resolves widget input, never gates web_fetch); tools.go:35-42 offers web_fetch whenever the webSearch family is on, tools.go:55 is the only mitigation (one prompt sentence), tools.go:59-66 makes the legacy /agui path default web tools on; context.go:194-195 and records.go:109 default web search on for chat (webapp chat-operations.ts:99-104 does the same client-side); widgets.go:65-82 executes render_link_preview server-side by POSTing the model's URL to the metadata enclave. Neither the harness nor the pinned tinfoil-go (v0.15.4-0.20260828072713) ever sets X-Tinfoil-Tool-Injection-Check; callerAuth (main.go:280-297) adds only Authorization and usage headers. Websearch e3751cf: handlers.go:188-220 accepts arbitrary URLs with PIICheckEnabled:false and InjectionCheckEnabled=nil when the header is absent; service.go:184-230 hands URLs to the fetcher BEFORE any screening; service.go:236-251 turns nil into (enabled, not explicit) so shouldSkipForRanker -> CloudflareRanker.InTopBucket (ranker.go:137-155, host or eTLD+1 in the top-500k list) bypasses the classifier; service.go:360-364 is fail-open; fetch.go forwards URLs verbatim to api.exa.ai/contents with maxAgeHours:2; main.go:106-118 activates the ranker when CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN is set, which tinfoil-config.yml lists as a production secret. Exa's public docs confirm /contents live-crawls uncached pages by default and maxAgeHours>0 forces a fresh fetch when the cache is older (URLs up to 2048 chars, 100 per call). Metadata fetcher 8f0fd7e: NormalizeTargetURL keeps the query string and contextdev/client.go:68-72 scrapes with maxAgeMs=0. The model router's safeguards package is an AUP sidecar submission that skips tool messages, so it is not an injection screen either. I wrote my own library-level test against the shipped websearch packages (fetcher receives URLs verbatim with query strings intact before screening; safeguard consulted only for the long-tail host; explicit header disables the skip) and re-ran the hunter's loopback PoC in my own copy on separate ports with the shipped files unmodified: the harness auto-executed the model-chosen fetch, all 13 MCP requests carried an empty injection-check header, no classifier call occurred for the top-bucket host, the Exa stand-in received /contents with maxAgeHours:2 and crawled the model-chosen URLs, and the attacker log held the decoded system prompt (personalization, project document) plus a prior user message; the long-tail control was blocked; the link-preview channel forwarded the model-chosen URL to the context.dev stub with maxAgeMs=0. By the brief's own definition (attacker = malicious web page / prompt injection; data = prompts, chats, documents the product promises to keep confidential) this is a real, reachable, serious application-layer defect, distinct from the five known transport/attestation findings.

Production facts I could not verify: (1) compliance rate of the deployed models with injected instructions (PoC scripts the model; the brief's attacker model assumes it); (2) actual membership of github.com/medium.com/etc. in the Cloudflare Radar top-500k dataset (radar page returned 403; near-certain but unchecked); (3) Exa's crawl of attacker URLs with long query strings is confirmed by public docs, not exercised; (4) whether the control plane's genUI.enabledWidgets includes render_link_preview (second channel only); (5) efficacy of gpt-oss-safeguard-120b with the narrow policy for long-tail hosts. The fetch handler does not screen URL strings at all (PII check disabled, classifier only on returned content after the fetch), so the exfil target host need not be popular; only the injection page's host matters for the classifier skip. Hunter's PoC uses github.com for the collect URL, which in reality would have to be an attacker-controlled host; this does not change the result. CVSS sits at 6.1-7.4 depending on how model non-determinism is scored; I rate High for Tinfoil Chat with default settings because the data at stake is exactly the product's confidentiality promise and the attacker is remote and unauthenticated.

votes.reasoning: All code claims re-derived at the pinned HEADs and confirmed. confidential-tinfoil-harness 4c170c6: agent.go:115-127 appends every model tool call and runs execute()->invoke()->toolset.call() (195-274) with no allow-list, confirmation or URL inspection; tools.go:39 maps the websearch enclave's fetch tool to web_fetch, tools.go:55 is the only mitigation (one prompt sentence), tools.go:60-66 and context.go:195 / records.go:109 make web search on by default (legacy /agui path: absent forwardedProps means on, agui.go:190-191); widgets.go:65-82 executes render_link_preview server-side by POSTing the model-chosen URL to the metadata enclave. confidential-websearch e3751cf: handlers.go:202-204 calls FetchDetailed with PIICheckEnabled:false and the injection tri-state resolved only from the X-Tinfoil-Tool-Injection-Check header; service.go:236-251 skips the classifier when the caller was not explicit and the host's eTLD+1 is in the Cloudflare top-500k list (ranker.go:137-155), and service.go:360-364 keeps content on classifier error; fetch.go:29,128-144 forwards every URL verbatim to https://api.exa.ai/contents with maxAgeHours:2. Exa's public docs (docs.exa.ai, fetched by me) confirm: positive maxAgeHours uses cache only if newer than that, otherwise fetches the page, so an attacker-chosen never-seen URL is crawled and the attacker's server receives the query string. confidential-website-metadata-fetcher 8f0fd7e: client.go:68-72 scrapes any URL via context.dev with maxAgeMs=0; fetch/url.go imposes no query-string or length policy (64 KB request body cap). Crucially the classifier runs on the fetched CONTENT after the crawl, so it can never stop the exfiltration leg; it only gates the injection page, and that gate is skipped by default for github.com/medium.com/reddit.com-class hosts, is fail-open, and is a narrow LLM policy. The collector URL can be on any host. PoC: I copied the hunter's work tree to my verify directory (diff vs pristine repos shows only added PoC files, no shipped file modified), rewired run.sh to that path and ran it on ports 23311-23313: exit 0, TestPoC_InjectedPageExfiltratesConversationViaWebFetch, TestPoC_Control_LongTailHostIsScreened and TestPoC_LinkPreviewWidgetForwardsModelChosenURL all PASS; attacker log recovered the system prompt (nickname, profession, additional_context, project instructions, the project document text) and the SSN message verbatim via two Exa-crawler GETs; websearch stdout shows every harness MCP request with X-Tinfoil-Tool-Injection-Check="" and ranker.InTopBucket("github.com")=true with no classifier call in scenario 1; exastub shows POST /contents with maxAgeHours:2. Only the model is scripted. Threat model: the brief explicitly lists 'a malicious web page the user visits' and 'prompt injection' as attacker positions and 'read data the product promises to keep confidential (prompts, chats, documents)' as impact; the exfiltrated data is exactly the conversation context Tinfoil Chat promises to protect, and it leaves through Tinfoil's own egress to a third party (Exa/context.dev) and then to the attacker, with a normal-looking answer to the victim. Tinfoil ships an injection screen for this threat (websearch README step 3), so it is inside their posture, and the default popularity skip is a concrete defect in that mitigation. Production reach: the public tinfoil-webapp c061681 and tinfoil-ios cd5824e do NOT use the harness; they call the model router /v1/chat/completions with web_search_options:{} (webapp default webSearchEnabled:true, profile-settings-serializer.ts:299; inference-client.ts:635-636) and never send prompt_injection_check_options. The router (confidential-model-router 6494b7d) has the identical defect: router_fetch is offered whenever web_search_options is present (toolruntime/profile.go:55-63), auto-executed with no URL policy (websearch_options.go:192-206 only merges caller domain filters), the injection header is set only on explicit opt-in (runtime.go:306-307), and the sole mitigation is the same prompt sentence (prompt.go:16,77). So the finding stands for Tinfoil Chat regardless of whether the harness is live; its component attribution should be broadened to 'Tinfoil web-search tool pipeline (harness and router tool loops + websearch fetch)'. The link-preview channel exists server-side in harness managed mode and client-side on the router path (webapp LinkPreview.tsx:41-66 calls the metadata enclave from the browser with the model-chosen URL; genUIEnabled default true). Not a duplicate: the five known findings are transport/attestation defects exploited by a TLS peer or host; the earlier noted-but-unreported item is only the client-side image channel. Severity: strict CVSS 3.1 lands at 6.5 (UI:R) for the paste-a-link scenario, but real-world severity is High: no attacker credentials or position, full-context leak including project documents and personalization, scalable persistent poisoning of popular user-content pages, and comparable industry findings (EchoLeak CVE-2025-32711, Slack AI, Gemini markdown exfil) were rated High/Critical. Even scored strictly it is a solid, unambiguous Medium with a reproduced PoC, so it is not refuted.

candidate.attacker_position: Any unauthenticated internet client that knows a running sandbox's hostname (e.g. <word>-<8 chars>.box2.tinfoil.sh). No Tinfoil account, API key, permit, SSH key or disk key is needed. For confidential-ubuntu / confidential-debian (also authenticated: false) only port 22 is published, so there the tunnel reaches just sshd with measured keys: not materially affected. For any customer workload that sets authenticated: false (the schema default) and publishes ports, the same applies.
candidate.preconditions: (1) The sandbox owner, or the AI agent running inside the sandbox, binds a service on 0.0.0.0 inside the workspace container on one of the 16 published ports (Express/Next.js on 3000, python -m http.server on 8000, docker run -p 5432/6379/3306 postgres/redis/mysql via the sandbox's own dockerd, a browserless Chrome on 9222, a VNC/RDP desktop on 5900/3389). cvmimage DNATs those to 127.0.0.1:<port>, which is exactly what the shim's tunnel dials. (2) The attacker knows the hostname: in the default cert-proxy TLS mode every sandbox boot gets its own publicly-trusted certificate whose first SAN is the sandbox domain, so hostnames are discoverable from Certificate Transparency logs (inferred from the shipped defaults; crt.sh was returning 502 during this review so it was not confirmed against live CT data).
candidate.root_cause: cmd/shim/main.go:259-290 builds `validator` only when config.ControlPlane != "" && config.Authenticated; for the sandbox's measured `authenticated: false` it stays nil. api.go:248 `if validator != nil && (r.Method == http.MethodConnect || requiresAuth(...))` therefore never runs for CONNECT, authorize() returns true (api.go:284), and tunnel.go:63-99 opens a bidirectional TCP stream to 127.0.0.1:<port> for every port any container publishes (publishedPorts(), tunnel.go:26-48). api.go:304-307 only disables tunnels when authenticated is true without a validator. The sandbox's own CLI pins the enclave and checks the RTMR3 seal (tinfoil-cli sandbox.go:418-432, attestation.go:35-50) and sends an API key only if one is given (tunnel.go:57-66), so the owner-only property is enforced nowhere on the enclave side. Tinfoil's config comment (tinfoil-config.yml:44-49) and cvmimage's TestTunnelReachesPublishedPortOnly acknowledge the tunnel is unkeyed, but the README of the sandbox does not, and the CLI's `--sandbox` help ("which must be sealed to your disk key") suggests tunnels are owner-bound.
candidate.impact: Anyone on the internet who learns a sandbox hostname can talk directly to whatever the owner's agent runs on the published ports: read/modify data in password-less dev databases (Redis has no auth by default; docker postgres/mysql commonly run with trust/empty passwords), drive a dev web app or file server (python -m http.server exposes the project tree with any checked-in tokens), take over an exposed Chrome DevTools session (cookies, logged-in sites), or attach to a VNC/RDP desktop. Port 22 is reachable too but protected by the enrolled key. The agent sandbox has open egress and holds the user's working files and credentials, so a compromised dev service is a direct path to that data. Severity is medium because nothing listens on those ports by default and the owner must bind a service on 0.0.0.0; it becomes high for the common docker-in-docker database and dev-server cases.

Threat model: attacker = any unauthenticated internet client; needs only a running sandbox's hostname and a service the owner/agent bound on 0.0.0.0 (or via the inner dockerd's -p) on one of the 15 non-SSH ports. The hunter's key unverified assumption (hostname discovery) I verified from public CT data via certspotter (crt.sh was 502): 99 distinct <words>-<8chars>.box2.tinfoil.sh hostnames in the first 200 issuances, publicly trusted certs (Google Trust Services, Let's Encrypt) whose SANs carry the hpke./hatt. encodings exactly as cvmimage cmd/boot/cert.go builds them in the default cert-proxy mode; the shape matches tinfoil-cli's sandbox test fixtures. So the only gate, hostname secrecy, is void, and the 404/502/200 differential lets an attacker cheaply scan every sandbox for exposed listeners. Nothing listens on those ports by default (image runs only pubkey-only sshd, dockerd, cron, nix-daemon, enrollment API on 8080 which is not tunnelable), so impact is conditional on the owner/agent binding an unauthenticated dev DB (docker postgres/redis/mysql), dev server (next dev, python -m http.server), tokenless Jupyter, DevTools or VNC/RDP on 0.0.0.0; the sandbox exists precisely for that use ("what dev servers, desktops and databases bind by default") and holds the owner's working files and credentials with open egress, so an exposed Jupyter/DevTools/dev server is a path to the whole workspace.

Stated security model: it is outside what Tinfoil documents to users. cvmimage docs/runtime-policy.md:91-93 says published ports are reachable only "through the shim's authenticated, attested CONNECT tunnel"; tinfoil-config README:43 says "Other published ports remain private"; the sandbox README and the CLI's --sandbox help ("must be sealed to your disk key") never warn that every published port is world-reachable. The acknowledgement exists only as a comment in the measured config and relies on a secret hostname that CT publishes. This is CWE-306 missing authentication on the tunnel for authenticated:false workloads, a real Medium rather than a best-practice note.

Per-mode severity: (A) confidential-agent-sandbox: Medium overall, High when a password-less DB/dev server/DevTools/Jupyter is exposed; CVSS 3.1 AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N = 7.4 for that case (AC:H because the victim must bind such a service), AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N = 4.8 as the generic view. (B) confidential-ubuntu/-debian/-ubuntu-config/-sandbox-gpu: only 22:22 is published and sshd is pubkey-only -> none (SSH banner/host key only). (C) customer workloads with authenticated:false plus published ports: same as A; no public instance exists (sweep of all 100 repos found only the agent sandbox publishing non-22 ports). (D) authenticated:true deployments: unaffected (401 / fail-closed). Not a duplicate: findings 1-5 concern EHBP, TDX collateral, code-execution /snapshot, 3xx handling and TLS pin ordering; Finding 3 only shares the hostname-discovery caveat, which the CT evidence now settles for box2. Verdict: real, Medium, not refuted.

candidate.suggested_fix: Install a restrictive loader on every assistant render: `.textual.imageAttachmentLoader(<loader that refuses remote URLs or renders a tap-to-load placeholder>)` (and the emoji loader likewise); if remote images are wanted, fetch them only after an explicit user tap and through the attested metadata/doc enclave rather than from the device. For GenUI, render `render_image` as tap-to-load, validate `link_preview`/`render_image` URLs against an allowlist or user approval, and strip `imageURL` runs from streaming content. Add a regression test that renders `![](https://127.0.0.1:1/x)` and asserts no request is made.
candidate.unverified_assumptions: (1) Foundation's `AttributedString(markdown:)` emitting `imageURL` runs for `![alt](url)` is Apple-documented behaviour that Textual's README/demos depend on, but it could not be executed on Linux (swift-corelibs has no Markdown parser). (2) The on-device fetch was not observed (no iOS toolchain/simulator); the trace is static. (3) Whether the production controlplane enables the GenUI `render_image`/`link_preview` widgets was not checked (would require calling api.tinfoil.sh). (4) The exact prompt-injection payload that makes a given model emit the image was not tested against a Tinfoil model; the class is well established.

votes.attacker_position_assessed: Anyone who can place text in the model's context during an ordinary chat turn with no network position, account, or user interaction beyond normal use: (a) the author of a web page returned by the router's web_search/fetch tools (iOS enables them via tinfoilEvents [.webSearch] / webSearchEnabled, router activates the WebSearch profile when RouterOptions.WebSearch is set); (b) the author of a document the user attaches or adds to a project (converted to markdown and placed in context); (c) content shared into the app; (d) a malicious/compromised model. The injected instruction must get the model to emit a Markdown image whose https URL encodes chat data; the device must be online. The exfil GET goes straight from the device (device IP exposed) to the attacker host over default ATS (any https host). GenUI render_image/link_preview variants additionally require the controlplane allowlist to enable those widgets (unverified).
votes.caveats: Not a duplicate of any of the five known findings (a related webapp-side image/link-preview channel was noted in memory but never reported; different code path and fix). Verification is static only: no iOS/SwiftUI runtime exists on Linux, and the Linux Swift 6.2.1 toolchain's FoundationEssentials has no AttributedString(markdown:) initializer (I reproduced the compile failure in probe/mdprobe.swift), so neither the on-device fetch nor the Foundation parser was executed; the imageURL-run emission rests on Apple's documentation (ImageURLAttribute, interpretedSyntax .full default) plus textual's own README/demos that depend on exactly this behaviour. Unverified production facts: whether Tinfoil's served system prompt discourages image output (irrelevant to injection robustness but affects ease), whether the GenUI allowlist enables render_image/link_preview, and model compliance with a given injection payload (the class is well established, but the specific prompt was not tested against a Tinfoil model). Minor: the hunter's example payload uses empty alt text `![](...)`; textual's demo uses the same form, but `![x](url)` is the safe form if Foundation drops empty-alt runs. Severity: High on the web-content/document prompt-injection position (CVSS 7.5 if the ordinary chat turn is treated as UI:N); a stricter reading counting the user's turn as UI:R gives 6.5 and adding AC:H for model compliance gives 5.9, i.e. Medium-High borderline, but the impact (silent exfiltration of chat content, attachments and personalization profile from a product whose core promise is that nobody outside the enclave can read chats) justifies High. URL length practically bounds the per-request payload to a few KB, so exfiltration of very long chats is partial per turn.
votes.cvss_vectors: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N (7.5) for the web-page/document prompt-injection position treating the ordinary chat turn as no interaction; alternatives: UI:R = 6.5, AC:H/UI:R = 5.3

Parser: AttributedStringMarkdownParser.swift:44-52 uses Foundation `AttributedString(markdown:options:)` with default `MarkdownParsingOptions()` (full syntax); `.markdown()` factory (:85-93) is what `StructuredText(markdown:)` uses.

Foundation `imageURL` behaviour could not be executed on Linux (FoundationEssentials defines `ImageURLAttribute` "NSImageURL" but has no Markdown parser: `swiftc mdparse.swift` -> "extra argument 'options' in call"). It is nevertheless corroborated by Apple-platform-only code in the repos themselves: the app's SpeechTextProcessor.swift:50 skips `run.imageURL != nil` after parsing assistant Markdown with `.full`, and its test TinfoilChatTests/SpeechTextTests.swift:38 asserts `![picture](https://image.com)` disappears from speech text; textual's README:56 and Examples (InlineTextDemo.swift:15, StructuredTextDemo.swift:22) render `![..](https://picsum.photos/...)` in the default configuration; swift-foundation's FoundationAttributes.swift:292-300 documents the attribute.

So any URL the model writes, query string included, leaves the device.

Attacker position confirmed: web search is on by default (CloudSyncModels.swift:611 `ProfileDefaults.webSearchAvailable = true`; new chats inherit it at ChatViewModel.swift:2896; ChatViewModel.swift:1746-1753 opts into router web_search events; router toolruntime/profile.go:38-41 is the web_search profile), so the author of any page the router fetches can inject; attached documents are converted to Markdown and placed in the user message (ChatViewModel.swift:2542 via DocumentConversionService); a malicious model needs nothing. GenUI: GenUIStyle.swift:95-103 `AsyncImage(url:)` for any https URL, used by ImageWidget.swift:98/101/227 (`render_image`) and also by LinkPreviewWidget.swift:64-65 for the attacker-controlled OpenGraph `image` returned for the model's URL; LinkPreviewWidget.swift:116-119 posts the model's URL to opengraph-metadata.tinfoil.sh (Constants.swift:549). GenUIRegistry.effectiveWidgets gates only which tools are offered, from the controlplane allowlist (GenUIConfigService.swift) - unverified production fact; the Markdown path needs no config.

Not a duplicate: none of the five known findings concerns the iOS client; the memory note about a webapp image/link-preview exfil channel is a different client and code path (CSP vs. textual's loader) with a different fix.

Severity: in the brief's own threat model ("a malicious model output / prompt injection" is a listed attacker position; prompts/chats/documents are promised confidential) this is High: a zero-click, no-position, no-auth channel that carries chat content, attached document text, project context and the personalization profile off the device to an arbitrary https host, plus the device IP, on every render of the synced chat. Per-mode: malicious/backdoored model -> deterministic (7.5); prompt injection via default-on web search or an attached document -> depends on the model complying with the injection (6.1 by CVSS, higher in practice given the established class). Fix is small: install a restrictive `.textual.imageAttachmentLoader` (tap-to-load or enclave-proxied) on every assistant render and make GenUI image/link URLs opt-in.

votes.reasoning: I re-derived every code claim from the pristine tinfoil-ios clone (HEAD cd5824e) and a clean textual checkout at the pinned revision (5b20cd9 = tag v0.0.11; `git status` clean). All hold: 1. Library chain (textual 0.0.11): `AttachmentLoader.swift:60` sets the environment default `imageAttachmentLoader = .image()`, i.e. `URLAttachmentLoader`, whose `attachment(for:)` (URLAttachmentLoader.swift:24-25) calls `ImageLoader.shared.image(for:)`, which is `URLSession(configuration: .default + Accept: image/*).data(from:)` (ImageLoader.swift:20-22, 50, 76-86). The GET is issued before any content-type/decode check, so a non-image response still delivers the query string. `StructuredText.body` (StructuredText.swift:118) wraps every parsed string in `WithAttachments`, whose `.task(id: attributedString)` (WithAttachments.swift:38-47, 86-95) resolves every `imageURL` run as soon as the view appears or the text changes, so this also fires mid-stream. The parser is Foundation `AttributedString(markdown:)` with full syntax (AttributedStringMarkdownParser.swift:44-52, 84-93); textual's own README (lines 46-56) and demos render `![..](https://picsum.photos/..)` with this default configuration, and WithAttachments.swift:7-9 documents that the parser keeps `run.imageURL` for images. 2. App: `LaTeXMarkdownView.swift:28` renders assistant text with `StructuredText(markdown:)` plus only highlighter/citation modifiers; a repo-wide grep for `imageAttachmentLoader|emojiAttachmentLoader` returns nothing; no `![` handling exists anywhere; `rewriteAnnotatedLinks` (LaTeXMarkdownView.swift:263-347) copies non-citation links verbatim and streaming renders raw text; `StreamingResponseProcessor` strips only `` markers. Info.plist/pbxproj have no ATS key, so any https host is fetchable. The assistant render sites at MessageView.swift:454/684/720/788/2076 are as claimed. Raw `` HTML is NOT a vector on iOS (textual's InlineHTMLPreprocessor does not convert it); only Markdown `![]()` is. 3. Nothing upstream neutralises it: the router's citation emitter (`toolruntime/citations/stream.go:94-106`) writes links whose URL is not a known source through unchanged; the only injection defence is the system-prompt sentence at `toolruntime/prompt.go:16`. 4. Defaults widen reach: every new chat has `webSearchEnabled = true` (ChatModels.swift:75, applied at ChatViewModel.swift:1190) and `ProfileDefaults.webSearchAvailable = true`, so attacker-authored web content enters the model's context by default; `ProfileDefaults.genUIEnabled = true`. iOS talks to the router directly (no harness references), with `tinfoilEvents: [.webSearch]`. 5. GenUI variants also verified: `GenUIRemoteImage` = `AsyncImage` on any https URL (GenUIStyle.swift:95-103) used by `render_image` (ImageWidget.swift:98-101, 227); `render_link_preview` posts the model's URL to the metadata enclave (LinkPreviewWidget.swift:116-120) and then fetches the enclave-returned og:image directly from the device (LinkPreviewWidget.swift:64-66), an extra direct-fetch channel the hunter did not list. These widgets are offered only if the controlplane allowlist enables them (GenUIRegistry.swift:62-66), which cannot be verified; the Markdown path needs no configuration. Threat-model assessment: the attacker is anyone whose text reaches the model (author of a page returned by default-on web search or fetched, of a document the user attaches or shares in, or a malicious/compromised model); no account, no network position, no Tinfoil position, and no interaction beyond the user asking about the content. The outcome is a silent GET from the user's device to the attacker carrying whatever the model encodes (chat prompts/answers, attached document text, personalization profile per PersonalizationPromptBuilder.swift, project context) plus the device's public IP and viewing time; textual's per-URL cache limits repeats on one device, but every other device that renders the synced chat fetches again. This sits squarely inside Tinfoil's stated model: README.md:7 promises only the attested enclave can read messages, the app itself routes favicons through the attested metadata enclave "so citation chips never reach an external icon host directly" (LaTeXMarkdownView.swift:14-15), and the websearch README (line 11) says fetched pages are screened for prompt injection, so injection is an acknowledged threat. Duplicate check: none of the five known findings in /root/tinfoil-security-findings/REPORT.md concerns a client or prompt injection, so it is not a duplicate of a known finding. It IS the iOS sibling of draft Finding 6 in /root/tinfoil-review/report-additions-draft.md (webapp auto-loads model-authored images; CSP `img-src https:`, markdown-components.tsx:446-453) and is adjacent to draft Finding 9 (harness/enclave-egress exfil). Different repository, different library default (tinfoilsh/textual), different code path and a different fix (install a restrictive `.textual.imageAttachmentLoader`/tap-to-load, proxy through the metadata enclave, gate GenUI URLs), so it is a material variant, not a trivial one. It should be disclosed as the iOS leg of Finding 6 (one finding, two affected clients) rather than a separate numbered finding, with the webapp-only `?q=`/`#send=` delivery vector explicitly absent on iOS (onOpenURL at TinfoilChatApp.swift:60 is OAuth-only). Severity per deployment mode (iOS App Store build, default config; direct-to-router mode is the only mode): - Web-search/fetched-page/attached-document injection into a chat with sensitive context: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N = 7.5 when model compliance is not counted; conservative reading AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N = 5.3 (the user must ask about the poisoned content and the model must comply). - Malicious/compromised model output: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N = 7.5, but this attacker is partly outside the stated model. - GenUI render_image/link_preview variants: same vectors, additionally conditional on the unverified controlplane allowlist. Overall High, consistent with how draft Finding 6 was scored; the hunter's "high" stands. Not refuted.

candidate.attacker_position: The client's TLS peer. (a) tinfoil-swift SDK users that pass `baseURL` (an EHBP forwarding proxy): the proxy operator, on-path by design, no key material needed. (b) The Tinfoil iOS app sends direct to the router enclave, so the forger must be a WebPKI-certificate-capable on-path party for the router hostname (DNS owner, ACME validation on the enclave IP, CA mis-issuance, or an enterprise TLS-inspection root the device trusts) — the same caveat as known Finding 1's direct mode. The iOS recovery path through api.tinfoil.sh (ChatRecoveryClient.swift:168-196) is NOT affected because the app checks for 2xx itself.
candidate.preconditions: Default transport (EHBP, no TLS pinning on the EHBP session: tinfoil-swift seals bodies and relies on the response nonce). The peer answers a sealed POST with a nonce-less response: streaming: any 3xx status (300 reproduced; 302-without-Location unverified on Linux) with an SSE body; non-streaming: any status at all (500 reproduced) with a well-formed chat.completion JSON. No decryption of the request is needed.
candidate.root_cause: EHBP Swift's `responseNonceHex` deliberately passes nonce-less non-2xx responses through as 'untrusted diagnostics', but tinfoil-swift hands them to openai-swift-fork unchanged, and openai-swift-fork treats every status below 400 as a successful stream (StreamingSession.swift:159) and ignores the status entirely on the non-streaming path (MakeDataTask.swift:29-34 decodes ResultType first and only consults APIErrorResponse if that fails). SPEC §5.3 says callers MUST NOT act on pass-through bodies as authenticated data; no layer enforces it.
candidate.impact: Integrity only: the TLS peer can substitute an arbitrary assistant answer (text, finish_reason, and `tool_calls`, which the iOS app renders as GenUI widgets such as render_image/link_preview/message compose) for a sealed request. The prompt stays confidential (sealed request body verified to contain neither the prompt nor user_cache_secret). Unlike Go, the 303 POST->GET downgrade fails closed in Swift (missing nonce on the final 200), and 2xx-without-nonce and 4xx are rejected.

votes.reasoning:
I re-derived the chain from pristine/pinned sources and reproduced it independently in my own work directory (fresh build, hunter tests plus four of my own). Nothing in the candidate is wrong; it is a real Medium, so it stays unrefuted.

Version pins (public GitHub tag metadata via git ls-remote, since the pristine clones are depth-1): EHBP v0.3.2 = 8528a8d, tinfoil-swift v0.8.2 = 4988b05, openai-swift-fork v0.0.15 = c8f8383; tinfoil-ios' Xcode Package.resolved pins exactly these three, and tinfoil-swift HEAD 81e07a1 (0.9.0-rc.1) still pins EHBP exact 0.3.2 / openai-swift-fork exact 0.0.15.

Code (verified by reading, not from the hunter): EHBP swift/Sources/EHBP/Client.swift `responseNonceHex` (0.3.2 :251-263; unchanged logic at HEAD v0.4.0 :453-465) returns nil for a nonce-less non-2xx so `request`/`requestStream` hand the raw body back; tinfoil-swift EHBPURLSession.swift (0.8.2 vs HEAD differ only by `snapshot()`→`current()`) forwards that response to openai-swift-fork after only the 422 key-config check; openai-swift-fork StreamingSession.swift:159 marks only statusCode >= 400 as error and AsyncClient.swift:41-42 → URLResponseHandler.interceptAndDecode / MakeDataTask.swift:29-34 decode the body with no status check at all. tinfoil-swift has no TLS pinning (the `tlsPublicKeyFingerprint` field is decoded in Verification.swift but never enforced), so the EHBP session trusts any WebPKI peer. tinfoil-ios builds the client with `TinfoilAI.create` and no baseURL (ChatViewModel.swift:1746, direct to the discovered router), uses `client.chatsStream` when there is no recovery storage (:4368-4376, :4669-4672: signed-out/free-tier users, temporary chats, cloud-sync-off non-local chats) and `client.chats` for GenUI argument regeneration (:5884) and project image descriptions (:2603). The ChatRecoveryClient path via api.tinfoil.sh (:168-196) requires 2xx and EHBP rejects nonce-less 2xx, so it is not affected; I confirmed that too.

Reproduction (my run, Swift 6.2.1/Linux, same loopback raw-HTTP peer that never holds the HPKE key): hunter's results identical (300 streaming and 500 non-streaming forged bodies returned as the completion; 200-no-nonce, 404 streaming and 303→GET fail closed; two Location-less-302 tests skipped on Linux). My additional tests: non-streaming `chats` returns the forged completion for 300, 404, 429 and 503 (so *any* status, broader than Go where openai-go rejects >=400); streaming 300 with a forged `tool_calls` delta (`render_image`, attacker URL, finish_reason=tool_calls) is delivered intact to the caller, which is what the iOS GenUI layer renders; 399 accepted; 301/305/306 without Location are refused by Linux URLSession (-1011) before any body, Apple behaviour unknown; control 302→GET→200-no-nonce fails closed.

Threat model: EHBP SPEC §5.3 says callers MUST NOT act on pass-through bodies as authenticated data and §7.1 claims a MitM cannot forge responses; the Swift caller chain violates §5.3, the same framing as known Finding 4. The v0.4.0 conformance/SECURITY-AUDIT.md "status not bound" known-limitation note is absent from the 0.3.2 module that ships and assumes deployments rely on TLS or application semantics; tinfoil-swift relies on neither. Impact is integrity only and blind (sealed request verified not to leak the prompt or user_cache_secret): attacker-chosen assistant text or GenUI widgets shown under the app's "verified" state, persisted into chat history and re-sent as context on later genuine turns. GenUI side effects are limited to rendering plus user-tap-gated https/mailto opens (GenUIURLOpener), so no code execution.

Duplicate check: this is a sibling of Finding 4, not a duplicate. Finding 4 covers Go (EHBP Go client, net/http redirect handling, openai-go) and states "other SDKs are not affected" naming only python/rs/node; Swift was never examined, the affected code and the fix are entirely separate (EHBP Swift, tinfoil-swift, openai-swift-fork), the non-streaming mechanism is broader (any status), the 303 downgrade does not apply, and it reaches the shipped iOS app on its direct-enclave path. Fixing the Go finding leaves this open. votes.attacker_position_assessed: The client's TLS peer for the sealed POST; no key material, no decryption, blind forgery. Per mode: (1) tinfoil-swift SDK users with `baseURL` set to a forwarding proxy: the proxy operator, on-path by design (AC:L). (2) Tinfoil iOS app, which sends directly to the router host the atc.tinfoil.sh attestation bundle names: a party holding a WebPKI-valid certificate for that router hostname plus an on-path position (DNS owner, a CVM host passing ACME validation for the enclave IP, CA mis-issuance, or an enterprise/MDM-installed TLS-inspection root on the device) — AC:H, same caveat as Finding 1 direct mode. Additionally, because tinfoil-swift 0.8.2 takes the enclave host from the bundle without binding it to the attestation when no enclave is configured (Verification.swift verify(): host check only runs for a configured enclave) and never pins TLS, whoever controls atc.tinfoil.sh responses could steer the app to a host whose certificate they legitimately hold while serving a genuine attestation, becoming the TLS peer at AC:L (code path verified in tinfoil-swift; the Go verifier binary's bundle host validation was not examined). (3) iOS signed-in users whose turns go through ChatRecoveryClient (api.tinfoil.sh) are not exposed: that client requires 2xx and EHBP rejects nonce-less 2xx. Within Tinfoil's stated model: the product promises that intermediaries/hosts/"not even Tinfoil" can alter nothing, and SPEC §7.1 explicitly claims response forgery is impossible.
